claims: Hip Thrust is an upper-back-supported hip-extension task with the feet supported, a declared implement and load position, an owned top position, and a controlled return.
Band, barbell, dumbbell, kettlebell, plate, sandbag, and bodyweight loading are variants when support geometry and joint action remain the same; floor-supported glute bridge is a separate definition.
The family is classified as supported horizontal hip extension with bilateral or unilateral laterality, sagittal-plane hip extension, knee-position control, and trunk-pelvis stabilization.
Exact cards declare upper-back support, foot support, laterality, implement, implement quantity, load position, range, tempo, top-position standard, breathing, setup, exit, and dose.
The hip extensors provide the primary joint moment while the knee, ankle, trunk, and pelvis have supporting and stabilizing roles that vary through the movement.

The card tracks gluteus maximus, hamstrings, adductor magnus, quadriceps, calves, abdominal wall, spinal stabilizers, hip, knee, ankle, lumbopelvic complex, and upper-back contact without claiming isolation.
Hip-extensor demand is substantial and changes through the lifting phase; range, support height, shin position, external load, and top-position control therefore require explicit declaration.
The valid repetition finishes through hip extension without substituting lumbar extension, pelvic rotation, foot movement, or loss of upper-back support.
External loading and single-leg execution change physical demand and stabilization requirements, so difficulty is assigned per exact variant.
Score exercise complexity and physical difficulty only, derive overall as their maximum, and keep athlete experience or proficiency out of the exercise card.
External mass, band tension, laterality, repetitions, range, tempo, top holds, and proximity to failure jointly determine load and fatigue.

Track local hip-extensor fatigue, hamstring cramping, trunk-position loss, foot pressure, contact discomfort, technical sensitivity, setup burden, and recovery before other high-force hip-extension or sprint work.
Resistance exercise requires inspected equipment, stable setup, appropriate technique, supervision, and controlled progression.

Require a stable nonmoving upper-back support, level nonslip floor, clear working zone, intact implement and padding, secure plates and collars where applicable, and a controlled loading and unloading plan.
Resistance-training dose depends on load, repetitions, sets, rest, exercise order, training objective, and the ability to preserve technique.
Use quality repetitions through an owned range at a declared effort, with enough rest to preserve support contact, pelvis and rib control, foot pressure, top position, and equipment control.
Instruction should establish equipment, body position, action, breathing, and safe finish before load progresses.

Cue the declared upper-back contact, foot position and pressure, ribs over pelvis, controlled hip extension, owned top position without lumbar overextension, same-path lowering, and secure equipment exit.
Qualified supervision, correct technique, manageable resistance, and gradual progression are central resistance-training safeguards.

Stop for pain, numbness, dizziness, pressure symptoms, support or implement movement, loss of upper-back contact, foot slip, uncontrolled pelvic rotation, lumbar overextension, asymmetric range, cramping that changes motion, grinding, failed repetition, or unsafe unloading.
Hip thrust loading is used to train hip-extension strength and power-related qualities, but exercise selection and transfer depend on the objective and surrounding program.

Place high-load variants before fatigue-sensitive sprinting, jumping, or technique work when quality is the priority, and account for cumulative posterior-chain loading, local fatigue, setup time, and recovery.
Athletes need the exact support, foot, load, start, action, finish, breathing, and equipment-exit sequence in plain language.
Expose variant, load, range, tempo, repetitions, rest, expected effort, self-checks, symptom guidance, contact comfort, and safe loading and unloading before the set starts.
Hip-extension demand changes through the repetition, making setup and position observations necessary rather than relying on a top-position snapshot.

Coach support should verify support height and stability, foot distance and pressure, knee tracking, pelvis and rib position, upper-back contact, range, tempo, symmetry, load control, effort, and safe exit.
Resistance training should be individualized to body size, readiness, equipment fit, technical control, and supervision.

Accessibility options include bodyweight, lighter or padded load, a lower stable support, shorter owned range, bilateral rather than unilateral execution, fewer repetitions, longer rest, live or tactile setup assistance, and nonvideo instruction.
Barbell hip thrust and barbell glute bridge have biomechanical and muscle-activity differences and should not be collapsed into one identity.

Implement, load, laterality, range, tempo, pause, and declared support height are variants within an exact upper-back-supported contract; changing to floor shoulder support or a fixed-path machine requires a separate definition.
YouTube currently supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

Five representative candidates returned current oEmbed metadata and title-level family or implement matches, but full viewing, exact support and load review, captions, accessibility, cue quality, safety, and human approval remain unresolved.

assessmentSummary.identity: Upper back supported on a declared stable bench or box, feet supported on the floor, hips lowering and extending through an owned range, with exact laterality, implement, load position, tempo, top-position standard, and safe setup and exit declared.
currentCardFindings: The stable legacy slug is misleading, but the canonical name is already Hip Thrust and the slug remains preserved for identity stability.
Five active source definitions describe the same upper-back-supported action with implement, load, or laterality changes and should consolidate as exact variants.

Feet-Elevated Hip Thrust does not declare whether shoulders or feet are elevated, and Hip Thrust Eccentric Lower permits either bench hip thrust or floor bridge setup; both remain separate and quarantined for human identity review.
Inherited source variants do not declare support height, foot position, load operations, range, tempo, top-position standard, fatigue, stop, or delivery contracts and are not selectable.

Twenty-nine inherited YouTube links returned current oEmbed metadata; five representative candidates are retained, but none has been fully viewed, exact-variant approved, accessibility reviewed, or approved for publication.

alternateAssessments.name: Bodyweight Bilateral Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing external load preserves upper-back support and the bilateral hip-extension action.

alternateAssessments.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A padded barbell across the pelvis changes load magnitude and equipment operations without changing exercise identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Band Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared anchored band changes resistance profile and setup while preserving upper-back-supported hip extension.

alternateAssessments.name: Dumbbell Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A dumbbell across the pelvis changes load handling while preserving the same support and action.

alternateAssessments.name: Kettlebell Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A kettlebell across the pelvis changes contact and handling while preserving the same support and action.

alternateAssessments.name: Plate Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A plate across the pelvis is an implement and handling variant of the same upper-back-supported action.

alternateAssessments.name: Sandbag Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A sandbag changes load distribution and setup while preserving upper-back-supported bilateral hip extension.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: One-foot support changes laterality, pelvic-control demand, load distribution, and side-balanced dose while preserving the hip-thrust support contract.

alternateAssessments.name: Feet-Elevated Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: Foot elevation can be a surface-height variant only when upper-back support and both elevated surfaces are explicitly declared; the existing source card is quarantined because it does not resolve that geometry.

alternateAssessments.name: Eccentric Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: An eccentric emphasis is a tempo variant only when the upper-back-supported hip-thrust setup is explicit; the existing mixed bridge-or-bench source remains quarantined.

alternateAssessments.name: Barbell Glute Bridge
alternateAssessments.rationale: Shoulders and upper back on the floor create a different support geometry, range, setup, and mechanical task.

alternateAssessments.name: Hip Thrust Machine
alternateAssessments.rationale: A machine constrains the resistance path, support geometry, belt or pad, setup, and failure protocol.

alternateAssessments.name: Frog Pump
alternateAssessments.rationale: A frog-leg floor position changes hip rotation, foot contact, range, support, and movement identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Paused Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared top hold changes tempo and fatigue without requiring a new identity when every other exact variant dimension is unchanged.
